title: The Kettle Island Field Trip
sum: On a three-day class trip to a steaming volcanic island, Nari, Sam and Mateo measure, count and write their way to a display for the empty visitor hut, and Mateo learns to collect rocks without taking a single one.

cast.d: an eleven-year-old girl who keeps the group's field notes and hunts for the right word
cast.look: an eleven-year-old Korean girl with a short black bob, a yellow rain jacket and a field notebook with a bent cover

cast.d: a twelve-year-old boy who puts everything into tables and likes being right
cast.look: a twelve-year-old boy with curly brown hair, freckles, a blue cap and a thermometer clipped to his backpack strap

cast.d: an eleven-year-old boy who wants to take every rock home and ends up drawing them instead
cast.look: an eleven-year-old boy with short black hair, brown skin, a green T-shirt and a pencil behind his ear

cast.d: the island's volcano scientist, busy and a little dry
cast.look: a woman in her forties with a long gray-streaked braid, a sun-faded red cap, dusty hiking boots and a radio on her belt

cast.d: the class teacher, who counts her 24 students all day long
cast.look: a tall woman with short silver hair, round glasses, a navy windbreaker and a clipboard

cast.d: Ana's black dog, who does not do caves
cast.look: a black Labrador mix with a gray chin and a red collar

p: The ferry to Kettle Island took an hour and a half, and Mateo spent most of it hanging over the rail. Far ahead, the island rose out of the ocean like an enormous green bowl turned upside down. A thin white thread drifted from a notch near the top. Mateo pointed and asked, “Is the volcano supposed to be smoking like that?”

“It's steaming, not smoking,” said Ms. Bell without looking up from her clipboard, “and that's why everybody calls it the Kettle.” Nari wrote the word steaming in her new field notebook, under her first note: “Wednesday, west wind, sea the color of an old gray sweater.”

When the ferry bumped against the dock, a woman in a sun-faded red cap was waiting with a black dog sitting on her boots. “I'm Ana Reyes, and I study the volcano,” she said. “This is Basalt, and he studies me.” The dog sneezed, as if he had heard that joke before.

On the way off the dock they passed a small wooden hut with nothing inside except three empty shelves and a bare table. “That's our visitor hut,” said Ana. “People get off the ferry, look at nothing and get back on again, so by Friday your class is going to fill it.” Sam was already counting the shelves.

Past the hut, the beach was black, as if a giant had spilled a jar of pepper along the shore. The sand felt warm even through their sneakers. Nari scooped up a handful and let it trickle through her fingers, and every grain glittered like a crumb of glass.

Mateo discovered the pebble near the waterline. It was smooth and black and almost the shape of an egg, and it sat in his palm as if it had been made for him. When he was sure nobody was watching, he slid it into his jacket pocket. Basalt was watching, though, and so was Ana.

“Island rule,” she said. “Nothing leaves, not rocks or sand or shells.” Mateo felt his ears go hot as he said, “It's only one pebble, and nobody would even notice.” Ana did not argue with him, but she held out her hand and waited.

Mateo dug out the pebble, but Sam grabbed it first and bounced it on his palm. “It's about as heavy as an apple, so call it 0.2 kilograms,” he said. Ana pointed at the ferry. “About 9,000 visitors get off that boat every year,” she said, “so imagine every one of them going home with a rock like this.” Sam started to multiply in his head, stopped halfway and let out a long, low whistle.

Mateo imagined the pile on the dock, heavier than a car and growing every summer. He took the pebble back and set it in the very dent it had left in the sand. A small wave slid in, rolled it half a turn and slid out again, and then it looked as if it had never moved.

In a tide pool between two boulders, Mateo found something even stranger. A lumpy gray stone was bobbing there like a cork, and when he poked it, it dipped under and popped back up. “Rocks don't float,” he said. “Everybody knows that.”

“That one does,” said Ana, and she fished it out and handed it to Nari, who nearly dropped it because it weighed almost nothing. Up close, the stone was full of tiny holes, like a sponge that had turned into rock. “It's called pumice,” said Ana. “The lava it came from was fizzing with gas like a shaken soda, and it cooled so quickly that the bubbles were trapped inside.”

Nari tried to describe the pumice in her notebook. Her first try, “Gray rock, very light, floats,” sounded like the label on a jar, so she crossed it out. Her second try said, “A rock that forgot how to be heavy.” Ana read it over her shoulder and raised one eyebrow, which Nari decided was a good sign.

Mateo returned the pumice to its pool, but he still wanted something to take home. Nari tapped the cover of his empty field notebook and said, “Collect it in there.” So Mateo sat on a boulder and drew the black pebble resting in its dent by the water. Across the top he printed ROCK #1 — STILL ON THE BEACH.

art.s: On a black sand beach, a boy sits on a boulder drawing a black egg-shaped pebble in his notebook, while a girl in a yellow rain jacket holds a light gray pumice stone and a black dog watches, with a green volcanic island peak and a thin thread of steam in the distance.

q.q: Why did the gray rock float in the tide pool?
c: The salty water held it up
The sun had warmed it up
It was full of tiny gas bubbles
It was made of black sand
q.e: The pumice cooled so fast that its gas bubbles got trapped. It is mostly holes, so it floats like a cork.

q.q: Draw Mateo's face when Ana held out her hand for the pebble. Give him a speech bubble with what he said.
look: Mateo looking embarrassed, maybe with red ears
a speech bubble saying it's only one pebble
q.e: Hot ears and a small excuse. You showed just how Mateo felt!

q.q: Sam guessed the pebble weighed 0.2 kilograms. If all 9,000 visitors took one like it, how many kilograms would leave the island each year?
q.a: 9,000 × 0.2 = 1,800. About 1,800 kilograms of rock would leave the island every year, which is heavier than a car.
q.e: Two tenths of 9,000 is 1,800. One little pebble each adds up fast!

eps.t: The Kettle Puts On a Hat
p: At eight o'clock on Thursday morning, the top of the Kettle was perfectly clear. Sam stood on the beach with a thermometer clipped to his backpack strap. In his notebook he had drawn a table with one row for every stop between the beach and the rim, which was 900 meters up. On the beach the thermometer read 24 degrees, so he recorded it in the first box and snapped the notebook shut like a spy.

Ana had one piece of advice for the whole class. “Bring a jacket,” she said, “because it's warm down here, and it won't be warm up there.” Mateo looked at the sun, then at his T-shirt, and left his jacket on his bunk.

The path climbed through ferns taller than their teacher and then out onto open slopes of red cinders that crunched like stale cornflakes. At 300 meters the thermometer read 22 degrees, and at 600 meters it read 20. “Two degrees colder every 300 meters,” said Sam, “like walking down a staircase, except we're going up.” Mateo decided that 20 degrees was still T-shirt weather.

Nari kept looking up instead of down. Around ten o'clock a small white puff appeared above the summit like a lost cotton ball, and by eleven it was spreading over the rim. She tugged Ana's sleeve. “Is that the Kettle's steam, sitting right on our crater?”

“That's a cloud, and the mountain is making it,” said Ana. She pointed back down at the ocean, flat and shining far below. “The sun warms the damp air over the water, and the wind pushes it up these slopes.” Nari looked up the trail and asked, “So it gets colder as it climbs?” “Colder and colder,” said Ana. “Cold air can't hold as much water vapor, so the extra turns into tiny drops, billions of them, every afternoon.”

The last climb went straight into the white. One minute there was sunshine on their arms, and the next the air was gray and damp. The drops were so tiny that they did not fall but simply hung there. Nari could see Sam's back, then only his backpack, then nothing but his voice. Mateo's arms came up in goosebumps, but he did not say one word about his jacket.

At the rim, the thermometer would not sit still. The numbers dropped whenever a gust blew and climbed again whenever the cloud thinned. Sam wanted one fair number for his table, so he took a reading once a minute for four minutes: 16, 19, 17 and 20. Then he chewed his pencil and started adding in the margin.

The crater should have been right below them. They could hear it hissing off to the left like a bicycle tire going flat, and they could smell it too, like rotten eggs. But all they could see was white. “We climbed for three hours,” said Mateo, “to look at a sheet of paper.”

Ana dug a spare fleece out of her pack and handed it to him without a word. It came down past his knees and smelled strongly of dog, but Mateo zipped it up to his chin anyway. Basalt sniffed the sleeve and wagged his approval.

Nari wrote with her hood up while the page went soft and damp. Her first sentence for the visitor hut, “The mountain had a cloud on it,” came out flat, so she scratched it out. “At eight o'clock the Kettle was bald,” she wrote instead. “By noon it had pulled on a white wool hat, and we were inside the hat.” Mateo read it over her shoulder and laughed so hard that he forgot to shiver.

They ate their sandwiches on the cold rim and waited. Then, for about half a minute, the wind tore a hole in the cloud. Below them opened an enormous round bowl, green around the edges and brown in the middle. A thread of steam was rising from a crack in the far wall, and everybody shouted at once. By the time the hole closed, Mateo had drawn the whole crater in eleven quick lines. Across the top he printed ROCK #2 — TOO BIG FOR A POCKET.

art.s: Three children stand on a volcano's crater rim inside a white cloud, one boy wearing a gray fleece that hangs past his knees, as a gap in the cloud shows a round green crater below with a thin thread of steam.

q.q: At the rim, Sam wrote down 16, 19, 17 and 20 degrees. What is the average of his four readings?
c: 17 degrees
18 degrees
19 degrees
20 degrees
q.e: 16 + 19 + 17 + 20 = 72. Share 72 evenly over 4 readings, and each one gets 18.

q.q: Why did a cloud grow on top of the Kettle by noon?
q.a: The sun warmed the air over the sea, and the wind pushed it up the mountain. As the air climbed it got colder, so its water vapor turned into tiny drops, and those drops made the cloud.
q.e: Rising air cools, and cool air lets go of its extra water. That's the Kettle's hat!

q.q: Nari wrote that the Kettle pulled on a white wool hat. Draw the picture her words put in your head.
look: a mountain with a cloud on top like a hat
tiny hikers inside or under the cloud
q.e: Nari's words turned a cloud into a hat, and so did your picture!

p: Late that afternoon, Ana led the class along the east side of the island to a dark opening in a patch of ferns. Cool air breathed out of it like the air from an open refrigerator, and stone steps disappeared into the dark. Basalt walked to the top step, sat down and would not go one paw farther. “He doesn't do caves,” said Ana.

A wooden sign beside the steps said LONG TUBE, 1,200 METERS, and under that, in smaller letters, VISITORS MAY WALK THE FIRST 400 METERS. Sam read it twice, frowned and asked, “We only get 400 out of 1,200?” “The rest is low and rough,” said Ana, “and you'd be crawling most of the way.” Mateo switched on his headlamp and said, “Four hundred sounds wonderful to me.”

Inside, the air was cool and still, and every voice came back a little louder than it went out. Twenty-four headlamps swung across the walls like a crowd of fireflies. The black rock was rough in some places and as smooth as a glazed mug in others. Ms. Bell counted the headlamps to make sure there were still twenty-four.

Sam ran his hand along the wall. “This is just an ordinary cave,” he said, “made by rain soaking into the rock and dissolving it over a million years.” Ana ducked under a low spot in the ceiling. “Rain makes caves in limestone,” she said, “but does this look like limestone to you?” Sam studied the black wall and did not answer. “Don't take my word for it,” said Ana. “Go and find me some evidence.”

Nari found the first clue about a hundred meters in. A thin ledge of rock ran along both walls at exactly the same height, and lower down there was a second ledge just like the first. They looked like the rings a bath leaves on the tub when the water drains away bit by bit. She wrote it down: “Clue 1: two bathtub rings.”

Mateo found the second clue on the ceiling, mostly by bumping his headlamp into it. Rows of stubby black points hung down like candle drips that had frozen halfway through dripping. He reached up to snap one off, then remembered the island rule and shoved his hand in his pocket. “Those are lavacicles,” said Ana, “left over from when the tunnel was still hot enough for the ceiling to melt and drip.”

The third clue was right under their feet. Instead of lying flat like a sidewalk, the floor was wrinkled into ropes and folds, like the skin on hot cocoa when you poke it. Sam crouched and shone his light along it for a long time before he said, “Okay, water doesn't do that.”

Ana stopped at the 400-meter sign and turned around. “A river of lava once ran down this slope,” she said. “The top of it cooled in the air and went hard, like ice on a river in winter.” Nari looked down at the wrinkled floor and asked, “And under the ice?” “Under the crust, the hot lava kept flowing for weeks,” said Ana. “When the eruption stopped, it drained out downhill and left this pipe empty.”

Then Ana asked everyone to switch off their headlamps, and one by one the fireflies went out. The darkness was so thick that Nari held her hand an inch from her nose and saw nothing at all. Somewhere far down the tube, water dripped, plink, plink, and somebody giggled. “Twenty-four?” called their teacher, and twenty-four voices answered, “Here.”

When they climbed back out, the warm air felt like stepping into a bath. Basalt thumped his tail as if they had been gone for a year. Sam opened his notebook to a clean page and wrote a heading: “Who made the tunnel?” Underneath it he wrote “Water,” crossed it out and wrote “Lava,” with the three clues listed below.

Mateo had already found a flat rock to sit on. On his page was a careful row of frozen drips hanging from a curved ceiling, each one a little different from the next. Across the top he had printed ROCK #3 — STILL ON THE CEILING.

art.s: Children wearing headlamps walk through a black lava tunnel with two ledges running along the walls and small rock drips hanging from the curved ceiling, while a woman in a red cap points her light upward.

q.q: The tube is 1,200 meters long, and visitors may walk the first 400 meters. What fraction of the tube is that?
q.e: 400 out of 1,200 is the same as 4 out of 12, and 4/12 = 1/3.

q.q: At first Sam said rain made the tunnel. What evidence showed that lava made it? Give two clues.
q.a: The walls had two ledges like bathtub rings, and the ceiling had drips of rock like frozen candle wax. The floor was wrinkled like the skin on cocoa, and water doesn't do that.
q.e: Three clues for one claim. That's how Sam changed his mind.

q.q: Draw how the tunnel was made, in two pictures: first the lava river with its hard top, then the empty tube.
look: hot lava flowing under a hard, cooled crust
q.e: A hard top, a river underneath, then an empty pipe. You drew the whole story of the tube!

p: On Friday morning, Ana took the class to a place where two lava flows lay side by side. On the left, the ground was a jumble of sharp black chunks, as if a truck had dumped a mountain of broken plates. On the right stood a forest of ferns and mossy trunks, with birds arguing somewhere high above. “Same volcano, same rock,” said Ana. “The one on the left came out about 200 years ago, and the one on the right is about 1,000 years old.”

She handed each group a square frame of four sticks, one meter on every side. Strings divided the frame into 25 small squares, five rows of five. “Lay it down on each flow,” she said, “and count every little square that has something alive in it.” Mateo stepped onto the young lava first, and it clinked and crunched under his boots like a dishwasher being emptied. The edges were sharp enough to slice a sneaker, which was why Ana had made everyone wear boots.

The frame would not lie flat on the jagged rock, so they wedged it between two chunks. At first there seemed to be nothing to count at all. “Zero,” said Sam. “This whole flow is dead.” Nari knelt with the hand lens from her pocket, and through the glass a gray-green crust turned into a tiny forest of curls and cups.

“That's lichen,” said Ana, “a fungus and a tiny alga living together as partners. The alga makes food from sunlight, and the fungus holds on tight to the rock.” Sam squinted at it and asked, “So is it a plant or not?” “Not exactly,” said Ana, “but count it anyway, because it's alive.”

They went square by square, with Nari on the lens and Sam on the pencil. Four squares had patches of lichen, and one had a tiny fern poking out of a crack, no bigger than Nari's thumb. Sam recorded “Young flow, 5 out of 25,” looking a little embarrassed about his zero. Then they carried the frame twenty steps into the forest.

On the old flow the frame would not lie flat either, but this time it was because of all the ferns. Moss covered the rocks like a green blanket, and a beetle tiptoed along one string like an acrobat on a tightrope. Only two squares were bare: one held a rock as big as a loaf of bread, and the other was a hole Basalt had dug. Sam recorded “Old flow, 23 out of 25.”

Nari asked, “Why are they so different, when it's the same rock?” “Time,” said Ana. “Lichen comes first, breaking the rock down a tiny bit at a time and catching the dust that blows past.” She peeled back a corner of moss to show the dark, crumbly soil underneath. “Moss grows in that dust, and ferns grow in the moss. Every plant that dies leaves a little more soil for the next one.”

Back at the edge, each of them wrote a card about the two flows for the visitor hut. Sam's card was neat and correct: “Young flow, 200 years, 5 of 25 squares alive; old flow, 1,000 years, 23 of 25 squares alive.” Mateo read it and yawned on purpose. “It's true,” he said, “but it's also boring.”

Mateo wrote his card as if the young lava were talking. “I'm only 200 years old, and all I've got so far is lichen,” it said. “Give me time, because my big sister next door already has a forest.” Sam read it twice and said nothing at all, which from Sam was a compliment.

Nari settled the argument with a roll of tape. She stuck Mateo's card on top and Sam's right underneath, so that visitors could laugh first and read the numbers second. Then Mateo sat on the edge of the young flow and drew one small patch of lichen, as big as it had looked through the lens. Across the top he printed ROCK #4 — HAS LICHEN, WILL HAVE A FOREST.

art.s: Two children kneel beside a square wooden frame strung into a grid on sharp black lava, one peering through a hand lens at gray-green lichen, next to a mossy fern forest where a black dog is digging.

q.q: Mateo wrote his card as if the young lava were talking. How was his card different from Sam's?
q.a: Sam's card only listed facts and numbers. Mateo's card told the same facts from the lava's point of view, using “I” as if the lava were a person, so it was funny and easy to remember.
q.e: Same facts, a different voice. That's why Nari used both cards.

q.q: Why did the old flow have so many more living things?
c: It got a lot more rain
It was made of a different rock
People planted it long ago
It had much more time to make soil
q.e: Lichen, then moss, then ferns. Each one leaves a little soil for the next, and that takes a long time.

q.q: Draw the two frames, each with 5 rows of 5 squares. Color the squares where the kids found something alive.
look: 5 colored squares on the young flow
23 colored squares on the old flow
q.e: 5 out of 25 is 20%, and 23 out of 25 is 92%. Your picture shows the difference at a glance!

p: The ferry home left at three o'clock, and at noon the visitor hut was still only half full. Sam's temperature table was taped to the left wall, and the two lava cards stood on the middle shelf. Mateo had torn his four rock drawings out of his notebook and pinned them in a row across the back. But the door, the first thing anyone would see, was still blank, so their teacher handed Nari a marker.

Meanwhile, the beach had turned into a problem. At lunch, half the class had kicked off their shoes and raced toward the ocean, and then they had raced right back, yelping. The black sand was too hot for bare feet. Yet the strip of pale shell sand beside the dock only felt warm. “Is black sand always hotter,” said Sam, “or is this beach just weird?” “Test it,” said Ana.

So Sam and Mateo set up an experiment on the hut's sunny front step. They filled two identical paper cups to the brim, one with black sand and one with white. Then they pushed a thermometer into each cup to the same depth. The sand had been sitting in the shade, so both cups started at 22 degrees. “Same cups, same sun, same everything except the color,” said Mateo, and Sam promised that the sand was going back on the beach afterward.

Inside, Nari was fighting with her notice. Her first draft filled a whole page, explaining lava and pumice and the island rule, and it even had two jokes in it. Ana read the first sentence and handed it back. “People getting off a ferry read about ten words,” she said, “so make them count.”

Nari crossed out a sentence, then a whole paragraph, then everything except one line. It still didn't sound right, so she tried it out loud on Basalt, who was lying across the doorway like a black rug. “Please leave the rocks,” she told him, and Basalt thumped his tail once. “Take a drawing home instead.” When he thumped it twice, she wrote both lines in big letters and taped them to the door.

After half an hour the boys read the thermometers, and the white cup said 32 degrees while the black cup said 42. Mateo stuck a finger into each one and pulled it out of the black sand much faster. He looked at Ana and asked, “Why is it hotter, when it's the same sun?”

Ana let a pinch of black sand trickle through her fingers. “This sand was lava too, before the waves spent hundreds of years grinding the black rock into grains,” she said. “Dark things soak up more of the sunlight that hits them and turn it into heat, while light things bounce more of it away.” She tapped the black cup. “It's the same reason a black car gets hotter than a white one in summer.”

Sam did the subtraction on the back of his hand. Mateo made a sign for the step that said FILL ONE BLACK, ONE WHITE, AND GUESS WHICH GETS HOTTER. Then they poured the sand back onto the beach and left the empty cups and thermometers on the step for the next visitors.

At half past two, the ferry appeared around the point and blew its horn. New visitors streamed down the ramp, and a little girl of about six ran straight onto the black beach. She came back holding a smooth pebble in both hands. At the hut, her father stopped to read the notice out loud.

The girl looked at the pebble for a long moment. Then she walked back down to the waterline, set it on the sand, and came back with her hand held out, palm up. Mateo understood, so he tore a clean page out of his notebook and gave it to her with the pencil from behind his ear.

The class boarded at three, and Ms. Bell counted them one last time. As the ferry pulled away, Mateo sat at the rail with his much thinner notebook on his knees and Nari's pen in his hand. Behind them the island grew smaller and smaller, green and round, with its thread of steam and its white hat of cloud. He drew all of it, and across the top he printed ROCK #5 — STILL THERE.

art.s: Outside a small wooden hut at a ferry dock, two paper cups with thermometers sit on a sunny step beside a hand-lettered sign on the door, while a little girl sets a pebble back on a black sand beach and a boy holds out a page from his notebook.

q.q: Ana said people getting off a ferry read about ten words. Which notice would work best on the hut door?
c: Please leave the rocks. Take a drawing home instead.
Welcome! We hope you have a very nice day here.
Rocks on this island come in black, gray and red.
This island has lava, pumice, sand and lichen.
q.e: Nine words that tell visitors what to do, and give them something better to take home.

q.q: The black sand went from 22 to 42 degrees, and the white sand went from 22 to 32. How many times as much did the black sand warm up?
q.a: The black sand warmed up 20 degrees and the white sand only 10. 20 is two times 10, so the black sand warmed up twice as much.
q.e: 42 − 22 = 20 and 32 − 22 = 10. That's a ratio of 2 to 1.

q.q: Draw the two cups on the sunny step after half an hour. Show which one got hotter, and why.
look: a cup of black sand and a cup of white sand side by side in the sun
the black cup's thermometer reading higher than the white one's
sunlight soaking into the black sand and bouncing off the white
q.e: You showed the one thing that changed, and what it did. That's a real test!

fin.q: Mateo never took a single rock home. How did he still end up with a rock collection?
fin.a: He drew each rock in his notebook and wrote where it stayed, like “Still on the beach.” His drawings went up in the visitor hut, so his collection stayed on the island too.
fin.e: Rock #1 to Rock #5, and every one of them is still on Kettle Island.

fin.q: The floating pumice, the tunnel, the two flows and the black sand all came from one thing. What was it?
c: Mud from the sea floor
Shells broken by waves
Lava from the Kettle
Sand blown by the wind
fin.e: Every rock on the trip was lava once. It just cooled in a different way each time.
